title: Limits — Concept and Introduction
notes: A function f assigns a unique element of Y to each element of X. If f(a) is a finite number, f(x) exists at x = a; otherwise it is undefined.
Example: f(x) = 3x + 5 exists at x = 2 since f(2) = 11 (finite). But f(x) = 1/(x−1) is undefined at x = 1 (1/0).
The limit describes the value a function approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a point — even if the function is undefined there.
Geometric interpretation: the y-value the graph is heading toward as x approaches a from either side.
Physical interpretation: instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.
Indeterminate forms (0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0^0) require special techniques — direct substitution alone is insufficient.
Key standard limits: lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (1−cos x)/x = 0, lim(x→0) tan(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (e^x − 1)/x = 1, lim(x→0) ln(1+x)/x = 1.
Algebraic properties of limits: lim[f±g] = lim f ± lim g, lim[c·f] = c·lim f, lim[f·g] = lim f · lim g, lim[f/g] = lim f / lim g (denominator ≠ 0).
confusion: Do not confuse limit with function value — f(a) may not exist while lim(x→a) f(x) does.
0/0 is NOT zero — it is indeterminate and requires further analysis.
Left-hand limit and right-hand limit must both exist and be equal for the limit to exist.
practice: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin(3x)/x using the standard limit.
universalFacts: Limits are the foundation of all calculus — derivatives and integrals are defined as limits.
Every polynomial, rational, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic function has a well-defined limit at every point in its domain.
The concept of limit bridges algebra and geometry — it allows us to talk about instantaneous rates of change.
